content: 1. A study conducted in rural Malawi found that the use of small-quantity lipid-based nutrient supplements in complementary diets did not significantly enhance child growth by 18 months of age. This was determined through a randomized controlled trial published in the Journal of Nutrition in 2015. 2. Research in rural Nepal assessed the effects of alternative maternal micronutrient supplements on low birth weight. This double-blind, randomized community trial, published in BMJ in 2003, demonstrated the impact of these supplements on birth outcomes. 3. In Ghana, a study revealed that lipid-based nutrient supplements increased the birth size of infants born to primiparous women. This finding was published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 2015 and corresponds to a Cochrane review study. 4. A randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind trial in Zimbabwe evaluated the effect of micronutrient supplementation on gestational length and birth size. The results, published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 2004, highlighted the potential benefits of such interventions. 5. In rural Gambia, prenatal lipid-based nutritional supplementation was associated with improved fetal growth. This study, published in Maternal and Child Nutrition in 2017, aligns with findings from a Cochrane review. 6. A randomized trial in rural Bangladesh compared maternal multiple micronutrient supplementation to iron-folic acid supplementation. The study, published in JAMA in 2014, examined the effects on infant mortality and adverse birth outcomes. 7. A comparative evaluation in Pakistan assessed the impact of multiple micronutrient versus iron-folate supplementation during pregnancy. The findings, published in Food and Nutrition Bulletin in 2009, demonstrated significant effects on pregnancy outcomes. 8. A randomized controlled trial in Guinea-Bissau investigated the effects of prenatal multimicronutrient supplements on birth weight and perinatal mortality. The results, published in the European Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 2005, provided evidence for the benefits of such interventions. 9. A double-blind randomized controlled trial in China examined the impact of micronutrient supplementation on pregnancy outcomes. Published in JAMA Internal Medicine in 2013, the study highlighted the benefits of these supplements on birth weight and gestational duration. 10. Research in Nepal evaluated the effects of antenatal micronutrient supplementation on birth weight and gestational duration. This double-blind, randomized controlled trial, published in The Lancet in 2005, demonstrated significant improvements in these outcomes. 11. A study in rural Burkina Faso assessed the effects of maternal multiple micronutrient supplementation on fetal growth. Published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 2008, the trial highlighted the benefits of these interventions. 12. The SUMMIT study in Indonesia evaluated the impact of maternal multiple micronutrient supplementation on fetal loss and infant death. This double-blind, cluster-randomized trial, published in The Lancet in 2008, provided critical insights into the benefits of such supplementation. 13. A cluster-randomized controlled trial in West Java, Indonesia, investigated the prevention of low birth weight through maternal multiple micronutrient supplementation. The findings, published in Food and Nutrition Bulletin in 2009, demonstrated significant benefits. 14. The MINIMat study in Matlab, Bangladesh, examined the effects of prenatal food and micronutrient supplementation on infant development. This randomized trial, published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 2008, highlighted the developmental benefits of these interventions. 15. A cluster-randomized, double-blind, controlled study in rural Niger demonstrated that prenatal multiple micronutrient supplementation had a greater impact on birth weight than iron and folic acid supplementation. The findings were published in Food and Nutrition Bulletin in 2007. 16. A trial in rural western China assessed the impact of micronutrient supplementation during pregnancy on birth weight, gestational duration, and perinatal mortality. Published in BMJ in 2008, the study provided evidence for the benefits of these interventions. 17. A meta-analysis of 17 randomized trials in lowand middle-income countries examined the modifiers of maternal multiple micronutrient supplementation effects on stillbirth, birth outcomes, and infant mortality. Published in The Lancet Global Health in 2017, the analysis provided comprehensive insights. 18. New evidence suggests that WHO guidelines on multiple micronutrient supplementation during pregnancy should be updated. This recommendation was published in the Journal of Nutrition in 2019. 19. A study in Tanzania evaluated the effects of vitamins on perinatal outcomes among HIV-negative women. Published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2007, the research highlighted the benefits of vitamin supplementation. 20. A systematic review and meta-analysis examined the long-term health benefits of maternal antenatal multiple micronutrient supplementation for children. Published in BMC Medicine in 2016, the study emphasized the importance of these interventions. 21. Modeling results from three high-burden Asian countries demonstrated that multiple micronutrient supplements are more cost-effective than iron and folic acid. This analysis, published in the Journal of Nutrition in 2019, highlighted the economic advantages of these interventions. 22. A study in Bangladesh and Burkina Faso evaluated the costs, impacts, and cost-effectiveness of replacing iron-folic acid with multiple micronutrient supplements among pregnant women. Published in the Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences in 2019, the findings supported the transition to multiple micronutrient supplementation. 23. A Cochrane review in 2017 summarized the evidence on multiple micronutrient supplementation during pregnancy. The review highlighted the benefits and provided recommendations for implementation. 24. A study in lowand middle-income countries analyzed the use and misuse of cost-effectiveness analysis thresholds in cost-per-DALY studies. Published in Value in Health in 2018, the research emphasized the need for appropriate thresholds. 25. A discussion on the pros and cons of cost-effectiveness thresholds was published in the Bulletin of the World Health Organization in 2016. The article provided insights into the implications of these thresholds for health interventions.
